chapter: Friends, New York life and recording routine
title: Bertha Chippie Hill and Johnny Dodds
summary: She recalls Chippie Hill at the Okeh night, a dance called the Mess-Around, and Hill singing her "Shorty George Blues".

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Why not? Sure. I think Bertha Chippie Hill was at that big night.
She was.
Do you remember her there that night?
______. I said, "Where did she get that name from?" I believed she was trying to copy my name.
Oh, yeah?
Uh-huh. She ______. She played "______ How to do the Mess-Around."
Oh.
(Unintelligible). "The Mess-Around."
She taught you that?
No, she taught (unintelligible) when I
was up there singing "Shorty George," she told me to sing "Do the Mess-Around," but I didn't do it.
Why'd she tell you to do that?
She was trying to -- it was a new (unintelligible). But it was a kind of a dance.
The "Mess-Around."
The "Mess-Around," uh-huh. Something like "Ballin' the Jack," you know.
"Ballin' the Jack," yeah.
Uh-huh.
What kind of a singer would you call her? How would you describe the kind of singer she was?

You know one thing, I ain't never heard none of Bertha Chippie Hill's songs in my life. She sang my "Shorty George Blues." She asked me to let her sing (unintelligible), but it didn't go nowhere (unintelligible), but it didn't go nowhere. My record was the one made good.
Well, she sang the blues.
Uh-huh, she sang the blues. But I (unintelligible).
Johnny Dodge (PHONETIC) was on some of those records you made. Johnny Dodge, --
Yeah.
-- playing the clarinet.
Yeah.
Do you remember what kind of a man he was? Remember Johnny Dodge?
(Unintelligible). I must know that name. Yeah, I must know (inaudible).
